sections.content: C. Informal Action - Step 1

If a member of the bargaining unit feels he has a grievance, he shall first discuss the matter in good faith with his immediate supervisor in an effort to resolve the problem informally. This informal action shall take place within twenty (20) duty days after the grievant knew, or should have known, of the incident which is the basis of the grievance. In this informal action, the grievant shall verbally advise his supervisor of the particular section of the Contract alleged to have been violated. The immediate supervisor will respond verbally within six (6) duty days after the informal meeting.

sections.content: D. Formal Procedure 1. Step 2

If the informal action does not resolve the grievance satisfactorily, the grievant shall have the right to lodge a written grievance with his immediate supervisor within six (6) duty days following the verbal response of the supervisor. If such grievance is not lodged within six (6) duty days following conclusion of the informal action above, the right to proceed with the grievance procedure for this incident is waived. The written grievance shall be on a standard form as contained in the appendices to this Contract and shall contain a concise statement of the facts upon which the grievance is based and a reference to the specific section of the Contract which is allegedly violated. A copy of the grievance shall be filed by the grievant with the Association. A response shall be made by the immediate supervisor, in writing, within six (6) duty days after the receipt of said grievance by the immediate supervisor. Copies shall be sent by the immediate supervisor to the Superintendent and the Association.

The primary use of the supplement shall be for supervision of students before and after the student day, and may include such things as bus duty, yard duty, hall duty, safety patrol and similar activities. If used for duties not similar to the above, the principal must secure approval in writing from the Superintendent or his designee. Teachers shall be notified of use of these supplements in their schools. If no teacher accepts the supplement, it may be offered to other school employees. In assigning special duty supplements, the principal shall make reasonable efforts to assure that responsibilities are equitably related to other special duty supplements and responsibilities within the school.

category_summaries.summary: The Board recognizes and acknowledges the Orange County Classroom Teachers Association, Inc. as the exclusive bargaining agent for the teachers’ bargaining unit, which is defined per the Public Employees Relations Commission in Case No. 8H-RC-754-1039 (Certificate No. 27). All other positions are excluded, subject to PERC clarification of job titles and any new titles within the unit, and neither party controls the other’s selection of bargaining representatives. Upon request, the Board provides the Association a work-location listing of teachers newly hired in the system, and it may deduct Association dues (including uniform assessments) from the salaries of teachers who authorize deductions in writing; dues deductions begin with the first full pay period after receipt of the authorization form, proceed year-to-year until revocation, are made in the amount of 1/20 of the appropriate annual dues in regular paychecks, and are not made in any event from a teacher’s pay. The Board must certify changes in dues amounts to the payroll administrator and transmit payroll-deducted dues to the Association on prescribed schedules (last day of the month and the 8th together on the 8th; amounts collected on the 15th and 22nd transmitted on the 22nd), with any dues collection shortfalls for employees terminating before total annual dues deduction handled by the Association. The bargaining unit includes teachers with equivalent certificates and specified successful service criteria, as well as temporary employees issued contracts, and it encompasses all employees defined in Article I; vacancies and certain recruitment details are provided upon request.

The contract terms tied to duration are effective upon mutual ratification and continue in full force and effect, unless modified by the agreement’s procedures. Items previously imposed by the Board, calendar, salary, and fringe benefits are automatically reopened each year, with the parties exchanging proposals for a successor contract by March 15 and commencing negotiations by April 1 (per Florida Statutes Chapter 447). Any tentative agreements must be reduced to writing and signed by the Board and the Association, and failure to ratify tentative agreements submitted before the Public Hearing renders those tentative agreements null and void. Contract modifications require mutual written agreement, and when issues are reopened, the parties either meet immediately or defer the matter to subsequent negotiations. Certain timing/renewal rules apply (e.g., notice of non-recommendation for annual contracts on or before April 1, and individual teacher contracts must be signed within 20 duty days). The contract includes specific extension/duration limits: guidance counselors and media specialists are notified by May 1 of availability of five-day contract extensions (including for the period preceding pre-planning), secondary cooperative method vocational education and agricultural teachers are notified by May 1 for summer-month extensions, athletic directors may be offered up to a four-week extended contract, and supplemental-coach duration is substantially similar and capped at 45 student contact days. The Board and Association may mutually extend contract duration up to one additional school year for specific program needs. If state law remains substantively the same, existing duration-related terms are not extended by interpretation, but the entire plan must be renegotiated upon substantive changes in law.

Under Management provisions, the Board retains and reserves its full authority, duties, and responsibilities for district management, and carries out its management responsibilities (including providing and coordinating major district services such as substitute teachers and custodial services). The Superintendent directs key assignment and appointment procedures (and may waive certain requirements in unusual circumstances), while instructional personnel are assigned by the Superintendent or designee; the principal (or immediate supervisor/worksite supervisor) determines staffing needs, staffing reductions/department placement, and may question/consult/direction as necessary. Teachers’ classroom control responsibilities are assigned by the principal, and teachers receive referral disposition information prior to/at student return; however, teachers are not required to perform specified additional duties (and certain roles, such as P.E. teachers who teach six electives, are not required to teach IMPACT or accept duty assignments). For transfers, involuntary teacher transfers require written notice five (5) duty days before the effective date, and affected teachers may present feasible alternatives before the scheduled change. Regarding evaluation/discipline, members of the bargaining unit are not required or permitted to participate in evaluating peers; summative evaluations for beginning teachers are solely the principal/immediate supervisor’s responsibility (and no peer teacher may perform those required beginning-teacher summative evaluations), though principals may still question a teacher and offer reasonable direction at incidents potentially leading to discipline. Principals also control curriculum implementation freedom, staffing/coverage decisions (including class organization and substitute use limitations—no full-time teacher as a substitute except emergency/unforeseen circumstances), and summer program staffing/program needs. Separately, management allocates and governs extracurricular/athletic and supplement roles through defined head/assistant coach allocations, athletic director and business manager responsibilities, trainer and band director qualifications/duties, and other supplement duties (including intramurals, military/cadet activities, and yearbook production), with limitations on assuming coaching responsibilities and with approvals/consultations required for particular positions and supplement use (including potential Superintendent written approval where specified).

Compensation provisions include salary placement and credit rules: teachers are paid on the salary schedule and are granted/updated experience and degree credits (including retroactivity to the applicable school year/date of completion), with verification required before experience credit is applied; no salary credit is given for substitute teaching (and for first-time Orange County employment, no prior teaching credit prior to the award of a four-year degree), and the agreement does not diminish salary credits for currently employed teachers. Pay timing and amounts are set by the salary articles/appendices: teacher salaries are as in Appendix A, with supplemental activities paid per Appendices B and J and placed on deferred pay status for 10‑month employees (paid 2/24 of regular salary in semi-monthly installments for 10 months, with the balance in a June 8 check); paychecks issue in equal semi-monthly installments (10‑month employees on the 8th and 22nd, adjusted to the last duty day if needed). Summer/session pay includes full-day pay when reporting in summer if insufficient students justify the class, summer employment at the daily rate, and final normal six-week summer program payments by August 8 (with equal payments on July 8, July 22, and August 8); stipends include $50 per day for required attendance. Daily-rate mechanics govern overtime/extended time (e.g., a 30-minute extension compensated within the same work week; scheduled work beyond a 7.5-hour day paid per Appendix G) and supplemental salary is excluded from daily-rate calculations. Mileage and other reimbursements are limited to Florida-law maximums (with tolls reimbursed on receipts and excluding round-trip mileage from home to base school), and mileage reimbursement is allowed without requiring use of the employee’s automobile. Terminal pay is provided upon retirement (calculated as the daily rate multiplied by 45% times accumulated sick-leave days), made available within 30 duty days, and payable to a designated beneficiary (or, upon death in active service, in the same amount); for overpayments, adjustments are generally corrected in the next payroll period and limited in retroactivity except where the teacher knew/should have known of the overpayment. Additional compensation includes stipends/supplements for coaching/sponsorship and other extracurricular or special duties (including specified amounts and rules such as assistant supplements at 2/3 of head supplements, supplement quartering/halving permitted where stated, caps on multiple athletic supplements for conflicting seasons, supplements distributed in equal monthly payments, correction/stoppage on the next check when conditions cease, and supplemental salary stopping/adjustment based on resignation/separation timing). Teachers assigned to irregular schedules (e.g., work between 5:30 p.m. and 7:00 a.m., weekends, or split shifts) receive compensation at 1.10 times regular salary; other special circumstances provide annual supplements (e.g., six-period legislative changes: $1,000; high school teachers: $300) and other supplement-derived compensation for extra duties.

Scheduling provisions include limits and notice requirements for teacher contact time and meetings (e.g., faculty meetings generally not exceeding about one hour per week except emergencies; any additional meetings must not conflict with previously scheduled items and may not infringe guaranteed planning time or duty-free lunch; parent/patron visits are scheduled at mutually agreeable times with prior principal approval). Teachers must receive notice of tentative teaching assignments, may be required to notify the principal if they will not attend open house, and must be given notice when flexible scheduling is used (a 30-minute flexible time block may be considered after consultation, with at least five work days’ notice, used only for required meetings on a specific day). Duty-day timing is governed around holidays and election days (duty day ends at close of students’ day on specified days; if preceding day is non-student contact, duty is six hours and 30 minutes continuous including duty-free lunch; election-day start options may apply). Staffing schedules must observe rotation/equity for supervision and limits on student contact (no more than three hours of continuous student contact; secondary teaching load capped at 1,500 minutes per week; assigned supervision rotated equitably). Planning and breaks are protected (daily duty-free lunch at least 25 minutes, and one hour on non-student contact days; daily assigned planning time—secondary/adult vocational equal to a student period but at least 50 minutes; elementary at least 300 minutes weekly with contiguous daily planning at least 30 minutes; certain elementary coverage protections and high school prep within the student day). Teachers leaving worksite during duty-free lunch are permitted, and attendance/check-in and itinerary obligations apply (teachers check in/out and leave daily itineraries; itinerant teachers provide weekly schedules). For irregular or extended schedules, use is largely voluntary and limited to circumstances like insufficient enrollment, with minimum advance notice by the supervisor, volunteer-first selection with fallback to least senior qualified teacher, advance notice of assignment duration, and limits on working time (including no requirement to exceed 37½ hours/week; two weeks’ advance notice for irregular assignments; option to substitute one shift instead of a split shift). Summer and school-year calendar scheduling is addressed through defined contract work days (196/216/all weekdays except nine paid holidays), Board posting of anticipated summer positions by not later than three weeks before the end of the second semester, a potential Board extension up to three days, and make-up of lost days by extending the school year if agreement on calendars is not reached subject to negotiations.

Leave provisions cover bargaining-team and administrative leave permissions (subject to principal approval for bargaining-team members), limits on the Association president’s leave status/insurance during the term, and transferability of unused sick leave days (including transfer on return to Orange County at 1 day transferred per 1 accrued day, up to 12 per year, and requiring the president’s assistance to secure credit). For the Association, members may use up to 75 leave days per fiscal year (with a 5-day maximum per teacher), and additional leave is discretionary with the Superintendent; the Association may seek substitute coverage reimbursement for substitutes other than permanent substitutes. Teachers may leave at the end of the regular student day and may depart during planning time/duty-free lunch with permission; itinerant/cooperative education teachers may leave as authorized, and no reasonable leave request is to be denied. Sick leave is earned (including 4 days with pay and monthly accruals), not capped for accrual, and may be used for personal illness, specified immediate family illness/death, pregnancy, physical examinations, and other permitted purposes; accumulated sick leave used during approved leave is deducted from the balance, and sick leave must first be expended where applicable. Long-term leave terminates June 30 of the fiscal year granted, generally may not be full-time employed elsewhere during the leave unless waived by the Superintendent/designee, and return/extension procedures require written notice by March 15 and timely submission of extension requests (with the Personnel Department responding within 20 days or 5 days after the relevant Board meeting). Personal leave provisions include up to 4 school days per year for personal reasons without pay deduction, charged to accrued sick leave and not accumulable; personal leave is limited in specific periods except emergencies, reasons need not be disclosed, and the principal may deny requests. Additional leave types include: professional leave (with pay up to 10 duty days, advance request at least 10 duty days, and with specific restrictions when students are in school; plus professional leave without pay for up to 10 duty days for advanced degrees at the beginning/close of the year), court/jury duty leave with pay (not charged to accrued sick/personal leave, with a litigant against the Board limitation for court leave entitlement), adoption/child-care/illness-related personal leave without pay (as specified), continuing/professional service contract leaves of absence (e.g., 1-year status), detached service leave (1 year with evidence of job offer), temporary duty leave (full pay with expenses borne by the Board when initiated by the Board), and personal leave without pay up to 12 weeks (plus possible Superintendent-authorized additional days). Annual leave includes paid 12-month employee annual leave (accumulable to 30 days), earning rules, scheduling requirements, and restrictions on using unearned leave; additional education/summer-school annual leave exists (up to 3 weeks per year, cumulative to 6). Military/Guard leaves permit up to 17 days per annual period without affecting annual leave time, with extended military leave without pay and reemployment for long-term military leave; the Superintendent/Board rules apply to extended circumstances. Sabbatical leave is limited to up to one year (Board-approved) with detailed eligibility, application timing (file by March 15), Board action deadlines (tentative by April 15, final by May 15), service obligation after return (minimum one year), enrollment/credit reporting requirements, and cancellation/conditions for noncompletion; sabbatical leave is not considered a contract breach/termination and does not count as a point. The Sick Leave Bank allows eligible bargaining-unit teachers (1 school year of employment and at least 6 accrued sick days) to enroll by donating 1 day, with ongoing replenishment contributions and withdrawal rules (21 calendar days to withdraw after replenishment notice), ineligibility until 2 days are accrued (and automatic assessment of 1 day), and restrictions on returning donated days. Bank benefits require personal illness/accident/injury, approval by the Personnel Department, minimum 6-day accumulation at time of need (otherwise repayment owed with up to 3 years to repay), and permits drawing up to 100 paid sick leave days, prorated in connection with Worker's Compensation (including eligibility while on Worker's Compensation or illness-in-the-line-of-duty after depletion of applicable days). Submissions for leave generally require forms and advance notice (except short-term sick leave and emergency unforeseeable absences where the supervisor must be contacted so substitutes can be arranged), leave is taken in full- or half-day increments, notifications include prompt supervisor notice and post-return certificates of absence, and teachers on leave are not required to perform work/recordkeeping/duty tasks during attendance.

Healthcare provisions require the Board to continue providing teachers’ health insurance benefits with no cost to the teacher for the “current health insurance program,” including coverage without deductibles or co-insurance costs to the teacher (with a stated $200 maximum individual deductible for the individual policy) and continuation of pre-admission and concurrent review programs (with a potential $350 total individual deductible if pre-admission program guidelines are not followed). A $5 per prescription charge applies to legend drugs and a $2 charge to generic drugs under a prescription plan, and a mail-order program is available offering a 90-day supply at $3.00 per brand-name drug and no cost for generic substitutes. A PPO option is available that waives deductible and co-insurance costs. The parties must meet to mitigate adverse impacts if changes are required beyond the Board’s control. The Board must include newborn nursery care during the mother’s hospital stay, provide documentation (copies of insurance policies) to the Association, and set the effective health-insurance date for teachers starting during pre-planning with a September 22 paycheck as October 1. For retirement, comparable insurance to active employees is available to those who complete retirement (subject to plan limits), with the premium cost borne by the retired teacher; a retired teacher-substitute option (for those not eligible for Medicare at retirement) provides extended medical benefits, with Board payment of the health-insurance premium, notice to the Personnel Department, and annual Fringe Benefit Committee review of substitute days needed to maintain benefits plus written premium-change adjustments to current program members. The Board’s health-insurance contributions must be combined and applied toward family coverage, and teachers may apply the Board contribution toward family coverage via payroll deduction; tiered family health insurance is to be discussed for inclusion in rebidding specifications. The Fringe Benefits Committee participates in bid specifications and has authority to submit proposed insurance-package changes, but cannot agree to changes requiring negotiations. Alternative coverage includes a voluntary HMO option negotiated with the Association prior to implementation and a voluntary alternative that replaces current health insurance if chosen, for teachers with group health insurance from another source, with unrestricted re-enrollment to the prior program (subject to normal new-teacher waiting periods unless the teacher would otherwise lack group coverage). Related healthcare-adjacent benefits include term life coverage equal to annual salary or $7,500 (whichever is greater) paid by the Board, plus continued operation funding and $150 per year per teacher for a multi-optional insurance program to purchase additional coverage. Benefits are not intended for elective surgery or normal maternity-related cases; termination upon death ends eligibility on the day of death, and where an enrollment period applies, benefits are retroactive if eligibility requirements are met. If a retiring teacher opts to forego terminal pay, an equal application of specified monies toward a health insurance premium is implemented by April 1, 1987.

Ancillary-related provisions include financial/credit and benefit treatment and administrative rules: the Association reimburses the Board 100% of any and all sums paid to or on behalf of the Association president; salary credit for half-time teaching, work experience tied to certification, and military experience may be combined, with any two half-years combined to form a year of credit occurring within a five-year period. For advanced degrees, a teacher must submit an official college transcript of record evidencing the earned degree award to the Personnel Department. Insurance and benefit payments are payable to the deceased’s estate, and if no beneficiary is designated, also to the estate of the teacher; the Board will provide payroll deduction options for obtaining long-term disability and additional life insurance, and free payroll deduction for tax-sheltered investments. The Board will purchase a retirement annuity for each teacher retiring early, with application/approval available prior to notification of anticipated retirement. A sabbatical-related note is cancelled and forgiven to the extent of 20% of the note plus all accrued interest for each year at the end of each year’s consecutive service following the sabbatical leave, and if the recipient dies, becomes disabled, or is dismissed, the remaining principal and interest is cancelled in full. Finally, membership in the Bank is voluntary, and future contributions may be requested when the Bank’s available sick leave reaches 300 days.

The Security-related provisions include: district-wide seniority accrues while serving as Association president. Expelled students under Section I.5 may not be returned to the affected teacher’s class without the teacher’s consent. Teachers must (i) submit required employment forms within fifteen (15) duty days after initial employment, (ii) keep a current valid certificate on file with the Personnel Department, and (iii) for contract purposes, treat regular vocational certificates as equivalent to a bachelor’s degree and advanced vocational certificates as equivalent to a master’s degree. Assignment and transfer security provisions require superintendent approval before placing members of the same family in direct line supervision, provide notice (and reason) of new assignments for certain reassignment situations, restrict involuntary transfers within the worksite from being used to discipline, and impose detailed vacancy/placement rules—such as posting bargaining unit vacancies, using rotations for peer-teacher assignments on an equitable basis, ensuring transferred/displaced certified teachers are placed before new hires for the same vacancy, and prohibiting transfers/hiring in a specialization area until the displaced teacher is assigned. Long-term leave return/recall protections require written notice by October 1 to teachers with expiring certificates, allow early return only when certified/qualified vacancies exist and prohibit new hires until early-return teachers are placed, and set time/notice parameters (e.g., Board notice to long-term leavers by February 15; recall letters by certified mail with a 15-calendar-day response window; failure to respond terminates recall rights; laid-off eligibility for recall lasts three (3) years). Reduction-in-force procedures use district-wide seniority and certification as factors, require specified layoff/recall sequencing (including continuing-contract recall first in inverse order of district-wide seniority and annual-contract recall based on favorable principal recommendation and seniority), and restore salary, fringe benefits, and seniority credits upon reemployment.

The Board must provide each teacher with an inservice-point record at least twice per school year. Teachers may seek approval for inservice-point credit for training that enhances competency, and if not preapproved, may submit a written request for approval to the Staff Development office; the record must list approved inservice courses and, when feasible, inservice hours not approved. Points are awarded for supervising half-time junior year interns on a schedule of five (5) weeks of supervision for five (5) inservice points, with supervisors notified at least thirty (30) days in advance when possible; points may be prorated if service is interrupted or completed by another teacher. Additional requested points require documentation from the peer teacher and principal. Peer teacher inservice training is credited at one (1) point per hour of inservice training. For middle school certification, no additional inservice course beyond the seven and one-half (7½) hour day and teacher work year is required, and “satisfactory experience” means eligibility for annual experience progression. Related administrative/professional provisions include: submitting applications in writing to the Superintendent or designee by April 15; completion of an Assessment Report must follow at least one (1) classroom observation and completion of applicable Observation Reports unless waived; reasonable assistance must be provided to help teachers correct deficiencies; transferred teachers receive at least three (3) student contact days of orientation and preparation at the new school during the student year, and elementary teachers whose grade assignment changes receive at least two (2) such days at the new grade level. Teaching/experience credit includes experience in other school systems (including college teaching), equivalent roles (guidance, media specialists, curriculum resource teachers), and Orange County permanent substitute experience; and additional credit applies where an advanced degree has been granted. Temporary duty may be granted by the Superintendent/designee if for school benefit or professional growth, and teachers may receive credit for coaching experience. Separate from teacher inservice points, appointment and training requirements include: temporary athletic-training supplementation for certified Florida teachers with academic background in specified health sciences and, preferably, student trainer experience; the trainer should be a National Athletic Training Association member, continually increase knowledge, promote/administer a student trainer program, teach the classes, be knowledgeable about sports injuries and taping/rehabilitation/triage, and be qualified as a first-aid/CPR instructor; appointed trainers must be active NATA members and actively working toward national certification, and certified trainers must maintain certified NATA membership. For band/choral instructional roles, after-student-day assistance and training are required; the Assistant Band Director must be certified in music education with a specialized instrumental music program and be responsible for teaching at least three music classes during the regular day; the choral director must have performed at least two (2) major concerts before the public.

The contract’s disputes framework includes notice and communication requirements (all official notices must be given as required by the agreement; address changes must be communicated in writing) and labor-relations timelines for bargaining proposals (both parties may select up to two (2) articles for negotiations each year; proposals must be exchanged by April 15, with negotiations to begin by May 1; any request for mediation allows for a mediator to be appointed). During bargaining, representatives must be empowered to reach tentative agreements; association bargaining-team members are relieved of regular duties, tentative agreements are submitted for ratification to the bargaining unit, and if tentative agreements are rejected, negotiations on those matters resume. Tentative agreements reached before/during mediation must be submitted for ratification prior to the beginning of any Special Master proceeding; if issues submitted to the Special Master are not ratified, they proceed to Public Hearing. Separately, “grievances” are defined as disputes over the interpretation or application of contract provisions, governed by a multi-step grievance procedure with specific time limits (including a three (3) duty day extension, written notice and waiver rules, and step filing/appeal deadlines), the opportunity for Association representation at each step, and rules on who may file grievances. The process requires good-faith informal discussions first, allows appeals from Step 2 to the Superintendent/designee (within six (6) duty days), then to arbitration if the Association elects to submit (within ten (10) days, requesting a panel of seven (7) arbitrators through the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service). Arbitration awards are binding; arbitration costs are shared equally, with transcript costs split only if both parties mutually agree to a stenographic transcript, otherwise the non-requesting party bears the full transcript costs. The grievance/discipline provisions also address meeting/recording timing constraints (e.g., grievance meetings held during the teacher duty day unless mutually agreed otherwise) and scheduling/appeal protections (including handling of administrator incapacity, and processing grievances pending at contract expiration to completion).

The Board and school administration must maintain safe working conditions and take reasonable steps, in cooperation with teachers, to provide precautions for teachers’ safety, including prompt written notification and forwarding of incident reports to the Superintendent, with Superintendent/designee cooperation (including legal counsel) in civil/criminal proceedings and assistance with law enforcement or judicial authorities. Teachers may use necessary and reasonable force to quell disturbances, restrain disruptive students, or protect themselves/others and personal or district property; physical force used for protection from disruptive students is not treated as corporal punishment. Corporal punishment is permitted only if the principal has delegated authority and the teacher consents, and only with another informed adult present beforehand and in the student’s presence. Teachers receive the Code of Student Conduct within the first ten (10) duty days each school year and it is reviewed with procedures; teachers may refer disruptive students using a principal-provided referral slip and, in emergencies, students may be sent immediately with a written report to follow. Teachers are required to report students they believe have contagious/infectious disease or headlice; such students are not returned to class until the principal takes appropriate action, and headlice/pinkeye/impetigo are not readmitted while a health threat exists. The Board must provide headlice shampoo supplies to sites and teachers at no cost for teachers’ personal use, must not require teachers to check for headlice, and teachers cannot be disciplined for refusing to work in an unsafe/hazardous situation with an imminent danger to their health/safety/well-being. Teachers cannot be required to search for bombs. The Board also provides first-aid supplies in each school, opportunities for CPR training, maintains safe/healthful working conditions, provides safe equipment/supplies, first-aid, first-aid supplies, special clothing/equipment/devices at no cost, restroom and lounge/workroom facilities (including non-student restrooms), and at least one outside telephone, free off-street teacher parking (with separate student/teacher parking at high schools). Related safety operational provisions include access controls for class visitations, visitor access restrictions where safety hazards may exist (requiring worksite supervisor approval and prior notice to the teacher), rules on releasing students only with principal/designee authorization to prevent unauthorized removal, and provisions for documentable inspections/observations and confidential teacher files. For athletics, the Board provides proper insurance coverage and workers’ compensation coverage for coaches/sponsors, arranges transportation and medical examinations/weight certification, attempts to prevent and care for injuries (including processing initial and follow-up injury incident reports and advising when athletes may return after injury/illness), and makes conditioning available if requested by the coach.

Miscellaneous provisions address contract definitions and document precedence (terms follow the incorporated Glossary; the contract supersedes inconsistent Board rules/practices; copy retention by both the Board and Association), annual reopening of previously Board-imposed terms, and use of outside consultants (costs borne by the using party). They require cost-sharing and distribution/processing arrangements, including sharing printing costs for 7,200 copies (Association receives 6,500 for bargaining-unit members) and various access rights (bulletin boards of 9–12 sq. ft. exclusive to the Association; additional board at Association expense; teacher mailboxes and exclusive inter-school mail use with restrictions on derogatory content; Association one-flyer-per-candidate allowance; teacher access to Board/state/FDOE policies; Board agenda packets provided Friday pre-meeting; official policy copies; public-record access and copies at cost if requested; and Association access to certain computer printouts—three sets per school year per specifications at no cost). They cover Association meeting/communications and administrative facilitation (substitutes provided for up to nine meeting absences; school facility use with required consent/cost-bearing; faculty representative announcement rights and voluntary attendance; exclusive bulletin placement location mutually set; office checkout/arrival procedures for the Association president/designee; teacher visits permitted except during student contact time/assigned duty with prior scheduling and placement arrangements). Miscellaneous employment/rights obligations include dues-deduction cancellation only after standardized forms are submitted, limitations on Board involvement in fines/assessments, possible revocation of dues deduction if the Association authorizes/sanctions illegal work stoppages, Board tort/legal-defense parameters (including public-meeting notice for defense expenditures and circumstances where teachers may waive Board protection statements), and teacher legal/document rights (access/inspection and no-cost copies of personnel/work-location files; confidentiality rules for portfolios, with beginning-teacher portfolio handled outside the permanent personnel file and transferred after completion). Additional provisions address logistics and operational constraints (no student/teacher fundraising drives without principal approval after Faculty Advisory Committee discussion; no teacher required to accept gate duty; teacher responsibilities for salary-credit documentation; and specific administrative/HR notice and posting timelines). They also address extracurricular/supplement-related governance in general terms (voluntary attendance rules for off-campus staff development except for required programs; requirements for committees, lists, and program planning; and various allocation/criteria concepts including minimum participants for qualifying service/interest clubs and program/contract performance expectations).
